name: BED
seoDesc: BED: work out α/β ratio from the dose rate factor and the BED. A free health calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: α/β ratio is what the BED calculator works out, and it gets there from the dose rate factor, the BED and the BED (biologically effective dose). It suits an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the BED calculator work?
sections.html:
The BED calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports α/β ratio in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the irradiation duration); then you type in the dose rate factor, the BED (biologically effective dose) and the BED (biologically effective dose) (2).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as < few minutes and > few minutes. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A plain number with no unit attached.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in grays. The unit chip switches it to any of the 5 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in grays. The unit chip switches it to any of the 5 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in grays. The unit chip switches it to any of the 5 supported units.

One field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the BED calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Α/β ratio=dose per fraction × total dose ÷ (BED (biologically effective dose) − total dose)
Α/β ratio=(-2 × EQD₂ + dose per fraction × total dose) ÷ (EQD₂ − total dose)
Total dose=α ÷ β ratio × BED (biologically effective dose) ÷ (α ÷ β ratio + dose rate factor × dose per fraction)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Irradiation duration set to < few minutes, α/β ratio = 10, Dose per fraction = 10 Gy and Total dose = 10 Gy. The calculator returns EQD₂ = 16.6667 Gy.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: EQD₂ = 16.6667 Gy should be roughly the size you expected from Irradiation duration set to < few minutes and α/β ratio = 10.

sections.html:

  • Shown in grays, and convertible to any of the 5 units on that chip.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Dose absorbed, opening in grays
  • Dose absorbed, opening in grays

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The BED calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the dose rate factor, the BED and the BED (biologically effective dose) — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the BED calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns α/β ratio, derived from the dose rate factor, the BED and the BED (biologically effective dose). Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the BED calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the dose rate factor, the BED and the BED (biologically effective dose), which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter dose per fraction in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Dose per fraction opens in grays and the chip beside it offers 5 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports EQD₂ = 16.6667 Gy. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the BED calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
